What Does a Community Nurse Do? Clinical Care at Home Under the NDIS

By Abundance Healthcare GroupLast updated 19 November 20267 minute read

The role, a typical visit, and where nursing stops and support work starts.

What does a community nurse do? In short, a community nurse brings clinical care to people where they live, so that health needs are managed at home instead of in hospital. This guide explains the role, with a focus on nursing for people with disability under the NDIS.

  1. Home
  2. Guides
  3. What a Community Nurse Does

The basics

What a community nurse does

A community nurse is a registered or enrolled nurse who provides clinical care outside hospital, most often in a person's home. The work includes assessing health needs, carrying out nursing procedures, managing medication, teaching the person and their carers, and coordinating with the GP and specialists.

Key takeaways

  • A community nurse assesses, treats, teaches and coordinates care at home.
  • Wound dressings, catheter changes and nurse-only medication are nursing tasks.
  • Trained support workers can carry out stable routines once a nurse has written the plan.
  • The NDIS funds nursing when the need is ongoing and comes from the person's disability.
  • A change in skin, swallowing, continence or alertness is a reason to call the nurse early.

If you are asking what is a community nurse, or what is community nursing as a service, the plain answer is nursing that travels. The community nurse role exists so that people with long term health needs can stay at home safely. For people with disability, that often means the nurse is one member of a team that also includes support workers, therapists and family.

How it works

A typical home visit, step by step

A visit follows a steady pattern: the nurse checks what has changed since last time, assesses the person, carries out the planned care, records what was done and tells the right people. A routine visit is often under an hour. A first assessment takes longer.

  1. Catch up. The nurse asks the person, family and support workers what has happened since the last visit and reads the notes left in the home.
  2. Assess. Observations, skin, pain, swallowing, continence or whatever is relevant to the plan.
  3. Provide care. The dressing, catheter change, medication or procedure that is due.
  4. Teach. A few minutes showing the person or a worker what to do, or what to watch for.
  5. Record and report. Notes are written the same day, and the GP, specialist or coordinator is told about anything that needs action.

Compare

Community nurse or support worker: where the line sits

The line sits at clinical judgement. A nurse decides what care is needed and carries out tasks that are restricted or unpredictable. A support worker helps with daily living and can follow a set clinical routine after a nurse has written the plan and confirmed the worker is competent.

TaskNurseTrained support worker
Assess a wound and choose the dressingYesNo
Reposition and check skin for pressure areasYesYes, following the plan
Change an indwelling or suprapubic catheterYesNo
Empty and change a drainage bagYesYes, once signed off
Change a feeding regimeWith the dietitianNo
Give feeds and flushes through a PEGYesYes, once signed off
Give medication that needs a nurseYesNo
Prompt or assist with packed medicationYesYes, under a medication plan
Write and review the care planYesNo

The routines in the right-hand column are what the NDIS calls high intensity supports when they carry clinical risk.

The basics

Tasks that need a nurse

Tasks need a nurse when they involve assessment, a restricted procedure or a decision that changes from day to day. The three areas families ask about most are wounds, catheters and continence, and medication. Community nurse responsibilities in each are set out below.

Wounds

A nurse assesses the wound, selects the dressing, decides how often it is changed and recognises infection or deterioration early. For pressure injuries the nurse also works out why the pressure is there, which may lead to a seating or mattress review by an occupational therapist.

Catheters and continence

Changing an indwelling or suprapubic catheter is a nursing procedure. So is assessing why continence has changed. Once a routine is stable, a nurse can train workers in daily catheter care and in a bowel care plan.

Medication and injections

Nurses give medication that must be given by a nurse, check that charts match what the prescriber ordered, and review routines after a hospital stay, when errors are most likely. A nurse can train a support worker to give a set subcutaneous injection, such as insulin, under a written plan.

Funding

How community nursing is funded in an NDIS plan

The NDIS funds community nursing as a disability-related health support when the need is ongoing and is caused by the person's disability. It is usually paid from the Core Supports budget. Nursing that treats a health condition, such as care after an operation, remains the health system's responsibility.

The NDIS has funded these supports since October 2019. If nursing is not yet in the plan, a nursing assessment that names each task and its frequency is the evidence a planner needs. Our service page for NDIS community nursing care explains how we provide it and what a first visit involves.

Why it matters

Signs a nurse should be involved and is not

A nurse should be involved when clinical tasks are being done without a written plan, when a routine keeps failing, or when the person's health is changing. Repeated hospital admissions for the same problem are the clearest sign that nursing oversight is missing.

  • Support workers are doing clinical tasks from memory or from a family member's verbal instructions.
  • A wound is not improving, or new red or broken skin has appeared.
  • Catheters block or bypass often, or urinary infections keep returning.
  • Coughing at meals, weight loss or chest infections suggest swallowing has changed.
  • Medication has changed after a hospital stay and nobody has updated the routine.
  • The person has been to the emergency department more than once for the same issue.

What you can do

What you can do between visits

Between visits, the most useful things a family or worker can do are follow the plan exactly, write down what they notice, keep supplies stocked and call early when something changes. Small observations, recorded with a date, help the nurse far more than a general sense that things are worse.

  • Keep the care plan where every worker can see it.
  • Note changes in skin, appetite, bowel routine, urine, pain or alertness, with the date.
  • Check dressings, feeds and continence supplies weekly so nothing runs out.
  • Photograph a wound only if the person consents, and share it with the nurse, not a group chat.
  • Call the nurse about a change. Call triple zero for an emergency.

Common questions

Community nurse questions

What qualifications does a community nurse have?

A registered nurse holds a Bachelor of Nursing and an enrolled nurse holds a Diploma of Nursing. Both must be registered with the Nursing and Midwifery Board of Australia through AHPRA, and enrolled nurses work under the supervision of a registered nurse.

Can a community nurse prescribe?

Most cannot. Nurse practitioners can prescribe, and a small number of registered nurses hold an endorsement to prescribe in partnership with an authorised prescriber. In everyday practice the GP or specialist prescribes and the community nurse gives or manages the medication.

How long is a visit?

It depends on the care. A routine visit for a dressing or a catheter check is often under an hour. A first assessment or a complex review takes longer, because the nurse needs the full history and time to write the plan.

Is a community nurse the same as a district nurse?

Largely, yes. District nurse is an older name, still used for nurses employed by public community health services. A community nurse funded by the NDIS does similar work but is employed by a registered NDIS provider and paid from the participant's plan.

Does the NDIS pay for a community nurse?

Yes, when the nursing need is ongoing and directly related to the participant's disability. It is funded as a disability-related health support. The NDIS does not pay for nursing that treats a separate health condition.

Can a community nurse train my support workers?

Yes. Training support workers is a recognised part of the role, and the NDIS can fund it. The nurse teaches the task, watches the worker do it and confirms they are competent before they work alone.

People often ask what do community nurses do that a good support worker cannot. The answer is in the table above: they assess, decide and take responsibility for the plan. If you are looking for a nursing agency in Sydney that works this way, or would simply like to talk to a nurse, we are happy to help.

Wondering whether a nurse should be involved?

Describe the situation and the suburb. A registered nurse reviews every enquiry and we reply within one business day.

Want to speak with a nurse?

Tell us what is happening at home. A registered nurse reads every enquiry and we reply within one business day.

Registered NDIS provider, Reg ID 4-JCLD6XE.

  • Registration is checked on the public AHPRA register
  • The NDIS funds nursing that relates to disability
